text: 7.1 Considerations for Generating and Assessing Evidence Being able to generate evidence to demonstrate the valid clinical association, analytical validation and clinical validation of a SaMD is essential to establishing the SaMD’s value for users. The degree of evidence generation needed for a given SaMD will depend on parameters including but not necessarily limited to the:  Maturity of evidence underlying the clinical association; and  Confidence in the evidence, as applied to a specific SaMD. The purpose of the assessment of the evidence is to select information based on its merits and limitations to demonstrate that the clinical evaluation evidence is high-quality, relevant, and supportive of the SaMD intended use. For example, an assessment of clinical association would classify a SaMD as having either a: a) Well-established clinical association: These SaMD have outputs with well-documented association as identified in sources such as clinical guidelines, clinical studies in peer reviewed journals, consensus for the use of the SaMD, international reference materials or other similar well-established comparators in terms of previously marketed devices / SaMD;

An example may include the combination of non-standard inputs such as mood or pollen count, with standard inputs such as gait, blood pressure or other physiological and environmental signals using novel algorithms to detect early onset of a deterioration of health or diagnosis of a disease. text: 8.0 Importance of Independent Review of a SaMD’s Clinical Evaluation SaMD categories are based on the levels of impact on the patient or public health where accurate information provided by the SaMD is important to treat or diagnose, drive clinical management or inform clinical management. For additional information on SaMD categorization, please see Section 7.0 in SaMD N12[2]. As part of the risk-based approach, and subject to individual jurisdiction’s laws, independent review of clinical evidence of certain low-risk SaMD may be less important and the manufacturer may ‘self-declare’ the appropriateness of the evidence. Again, subject to individual jurisdiction’s laws, independent review of clinical evidence of more high-risk SaMD is more important in providing users the confidence in the SaMD’s performance metrics, including but not limited to, identification of design errors or limitation, broadening technical competence, testing the appropriateness of assumptions, and management of bias.

text: 9.0 Pathway for Continuous Learning Leveraging Real World Performance Data SaMD may leverage connectivity between devices, and people to continuously monitor the safety, effectiveness and performance of the SaMD. A SaMD manufacturer may have a hypothesis about future functionality and intended use of a SaMD that may be informed by continuously collecting and analyzing data on use of the SaMD in a post-market setting. Monitoring real world performance data can help the SaMD functionality and intended use evolve after initial introduction into the market. Such data may include post-market information such as safety data, results from performance studies, on-going clinical evidence generation for medical devices, new research publications / results that support or strengthen the clinical association of the SaMD output to a clinical condition, or direct enduser feedback, that can help the SaMD manufacturer understand the real world performance of the SaMD. text: 1.0 Introduction Software is playing an increasingly important and critical role in healthcare with many clinical and administrative purposes. Software used in healthcare operates in a complex socio-technical environment—consisting of software, hardware, networks, and people—and frequently forms part of larger systems that must operate in a unified manner. This software frequently depends on other commercial off-theshelf (COTS) software and on other systems and data repositories for source data. A subset of software used in healthcare meets the definition of a medical device; globally, regulatory authorities regulate such software accordingly. Existing regulations for medical device software are largely focused on medical device software that is embedded in dedicated hardware medical devices and are focused around physical harm, transmission of energy and/or substances to or from the body, the degree of invasiveness to the body, closeness to sensitive organs, duration of use, diseases, processes and public health risk, competence of user and effect on population due to communicable diseases, etc.

It is increasingly being deployed on general-purpose hardware and delivered, in diverse care settings, on a multitude of technology platforms (e.g., personal computers, smart phones, and in the cloud) that are easily accessible. It is also being increasingly interconnected to other systems and datasets (e.g., via networks and over the Internet). The complexity of medical device software, together with the increasing connectedness of systems, results in emergent behaviors not usually seen in hardware medical devices. This introduces new and unique challenges. For example: • Medical device software might behave differently when deployed to different hardware platforms. • Often an update made available by the manufacturer is left to the user of the medical device software to install.

text: This document is focused on a selected subset of medical device software. This software is called Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and is defined in IMDRF SaMD WG N10 / Software as a Medical Device: Key Definitions. Definition: Software as a Medical Device1 SaMD is defined as software intended to be used for one or more medical purposes that perform these purposes without being part of a hardware medical device. The objective of this document is to introduce a foundational approach, harmonized vocabulary and general and specific considerations for manufacturers, regulators, and users alike to address the unique challenges associated with the use of SaMD. The approach developed in this document is intended only to establish a common understanding for SaMD and can be used as reference. This document is not intended to replace or modify existing regulatory classification schemes or requirements. Further efforts are required prior to the use of this foundational approach for possible regulatory purposes.

text: 3.4 SaMD Changes SaMD changes refer to any modifications made throughout the lifecycle of the SaMD including the maintenance phase. Software maintenance4 can include adaptive (e.g. keeps pace with the changing environment), perfective (e.g. recoding to improve software performance), corrective (e.g., corrects discovered problems), or preventive (e.g., corrects latent faults in the software product before they become operational faults). It is generally accepted that testing of software is not sufficient to determine that it is safe in operation. As a consequence, it is recognized that confidence should be built into software in order to assure its safety. IEC 62304 is a standard for life-cycle development of medical device software. The combination of these concepts allows SaMD manufacturers to follow a clearly structured and consistently repeatable decision-making process to promote safety for SaMD. An SaMD may also fail with changes to the running environment. Changes to SaMD or its operating environment can affect its safety, quality and performance. SaMD changes refer to any modifications made throughout the lifecycle of the SaMD including the maintenance phase. The nature of software maintenance changes can include adaptive (e.g. keeps pace with the changing environment), perfective (e.g. recoding to improve software performance), corrective (e.g. corrects discovered problems), or preventive changes (e.g. corrects latent faults in the software product before they become operational faults).

Abstract

Effective data governance can support countries in implementing a people-centred approach in their justice systems. It can help policymakers better understand the scope, nature and impact of justice problems, design and deliver people-centred justice services, and measure what works. This working paper explores the role of data in delivering people-centred justice, as well as the values, objectives and practices necessary for data governance to harness its full potential. This paper is based on desk research and in- depth interviews with national representatives and line ministries in selected countries and with private and third sectors. It builds on the OECD Recommendation on Access to Justice and People-Centred Justice Systems, the OECD Framework and Good Practice Principles for People-Centred Justice, the OECD Digital Government Policy Framework, and the OECD Data Governance Framework. It incorporates lessons from data governance activities and experiences in justice and other relevant sectors.

text:  7 The role of data in delivering1 people-centred justice Context Transitioning to a people-centred justice system requires re-designing processes and services around people and their needs. A people-centred purpose should strive to achieve equal access to justice services, information and outcomes for all. However, current attempts to deliver people-centred justice policies, processes and services are hampered by limited data on people’s legal needs, issues they have brought to formal justice institutions (their “justice problems”), or their experience as they try to resolve them. Investing in the collection, use, maintenance and sharing of data is vital for the design of justice systems that meet people's needs on an equal basis. The OECD Recommendation on Access to Justice and People-Centred Justice Systems and the OECD Framework and Good Practice Principles for People-Centred Justice (hereafter “PCJ Framework”) recognise that collecting, using, sharing and maintaining data about people, their justice problems and experience with justice systems and services is crucial to the design of people-centred strategies and to monitor their efficacy (OECD, 2023[1]) (OECD, 2021[2]).

text: out people, their justice problems and experience with justice systems and services is crucial to the design of people-centred strategies and to monitor their efficacy (OECD, 2023[1]) (OECD, 2021[2]). Data on the wider social and economic impact of justice problems and on the benefits to people and society when these problems are resolved are also vital for building a case for ongoing investment in people-centred justice approaches. The OECD discussion paper “Grasping the Justice Gap” (Chapman, Peter et al., 2021[3]), co-produced with Pathfinders and the World Justice Project, proposed three data priorities to strengthen people-centred justice: • Data to understand the scope, nature and impact of justice problems. Those in charge of designing and delivering justice systems need data to better understand who has justice needs, what those needs are, when and where they are experienced, their underlying causes, and their impacts and costs. • Data to design and deliver people-centred justice systems and services.

text: ustice needs, what those needs are, when and where they are experienced, their underlying causes, and their impacts and costs. • Data to design and deliver people-centred justice systems and services. This encompasses data that can inform the design and delivery of policies and services to strengthen legal capability, prevent justice problems, and correct systemic bias and injustices. • Data to measure what works. The justice sector falls behind other social sectors (including health and education) in evaluating what works to deliver better outcomes for people. Effective and appropriate evaluation of access to justice initiatives is key to adapting strategies, allocating resources and achieving justice for all. The different types of data required to meet these priorities are likely to be held by a variety of actors both inside and outside of the justice system (see Table 1). Typically, these data are held in different formats, subject to different definitions, and collected, stored and maintained by a range of statutory and nonstatutory services and agencies, across both the public and private sectors.

Source: Author’s own elaboration. Why do policymakers need new justice data governance frameworks to support a transition to people-centred justice? Data governance is one of the top policy priorities that governments must consider when seeking to maximise the benefits of data access and sharing and address related risks and challenges (OECD, 2024[4]). Effective data governance ensures that data are consistent and trustworthy, and that it is not misused. Data governance refers to the set of policies, procedures and rules that govern the collection, storage, sharing, use and maintenance of data. It encompasses a variety of arrangements, including technical, policy, regulatory or institutional provisions, that affect data throughout their lifecycle (creation, collection, storage, use, protection, access, sharing and deletion) and across both policy domains and organisational and

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: stitutional provisions, that affect data throughout their lifecycle (creation, collection, storage, use, protection, access, sharing and deletion) and across both policy domains and organisational and national borders. The OECD Recommendation on Access to Justice and People-Centred Justice Systems and the PCJ Framework recognise that delivering people-centred justice requires a cultural shift in the way justice services and systems are designed and delivered. Pillar 2 of the PCJ Framework recognises the need for effective governance to steward and cement this (OECD, 2021[2]). In this regard, a new justice data governance framework is required to: 1. Re-orientate existing data collection practices; 2. Identify and address constitutional concerns, including the rule of law, equity and privacy; 3. Manage the opportunities and issues created by digital transformation; 4. Support data sharing within and beyond the formal agencies of the justice system; and

5. Create mechanisms to ensure that justice data governance itself reflects the PCJ Framework.

Re-orientate data collection practices

It is important to expand the data collection practices of formal agencies of the justice system beyond recording the information that is solely relevant to the agencies. This calls for the recording of data that help justice actors to understand the pathways, experiences and needs of the people who seek to navigate the justice system. Digital transformation offers an opportunity to undertake this work, but new governance models are needed to co-ordinate and direct these efforts and ensure that relevant data are collected in the most appropriate format.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: The PCJ Framework notes that justice systems in most countries have evolved over centuries, often not in a people-centred way (OECD, 2021[2]). Similarly, a people-centred approach has rarely been adopted as a starting point for addressing justice problems. From a data perspective, this also means data have not been collected on justice problems that people face, the impact these problems have on them, people’s decisions when resolving their justice problems, their experiences with justice services, or their ability to obtain a fair outcome. By losing sight of the need to gather these data, justice systems may fail to address the real needs and challenges faced by the people they serve.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: International reviews of existing justice data governance practices have confirmed that policies, procedures and rules that govern the collection, storage, sharing, use and maintenance of justice data have evolved to reflect the current structures and priorities of justice systems. As a result, justice data governance is often complex and unsystematic. This leaves the benefits of justice data largely untapped, particularly its potential to better prioritise, protect and reflect the interests of the people who rely on justice systems for protection and fair treatment (Townend, J. and Wiener, C., 2021[5]). Given the current state of data governance globally, achieving people-centred justice often requires re-thinking conventional data collection practices and redesigning the way data are collected, stored and shared by the agencies of the formal justice system.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
Where data are collected, they are often held and stored in formats that are not easily accessible (e.g. in narrative format, PDF, or paper files), or recorded inconsistently across agencies. In addition, administrative data (e.g. data collected primarily for administrative purposes as part of organisations day- to-day operations) tend to be structured around the events that are most relevant to these agencies (e.g. cases and not individuals). This creates significant barriers to understanding the experience of the justice system from a people-centred perspective.

Identify and address constitutional/legal concerns that inhibit data collection, sharing and use

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: Even when data relevant to the design, delivery and evaluation of people-centred justice systems are collected and stored in accessible formats, there can be cultural, constitutional or legal barriers to using and sharing these data both among justice institutions and with the executive branch of government. Barriers to using and sharing data on user’s experiences in the justice system often stem from concerns about judicial performance management (e.g. cases in; cases out; case type; judgment delivery; number of cases assigned by judge; disposition rates; appeal rates), and the threat this poses to judicial independence or the independence of the prosecutorial function. This can result in additional pressure on judges to conform to certain data trends and excessive judicial scrutiny, and may create an environment where judges feel continuously monitored.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: Developing a new data governance framework that brings together stakeholders from the executive and judicial branches to identify, navigate and develop arrangements that resolve these concerns is vital to harness the benefits of data for people-centred justice. If designed with the appropriate safeguards, this should not pose any challenges to the independence of the judiciary.

metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)

text:
10 

Manage the opportunities and issues created by digital transformation

Justice systems were predominantly paper based until recently. The recent push to use digital technologies and data to transform organisations, services and processes has been a catalyst to improve people’s experience of justice systems. Yet, the digital transformation also creates novel issues that require consideration.

Digital transformation creates opportunities to rethink the way in which information about the justice system is disseminated to court users, the media and the public. Yet, the opportunity presented by digital transformation to collect more data in a format that is capable of being both analysed readily and disseminated widely also entails ethical, legal and policy issues. The issues include how to respond to requests for bulk access to data. There is a need to balance the principle of open justice with the need to protect the privacy of justice and legal services’ users, particularly people in vulnerable situations.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça
metadata.section_path: Manage the opportunities and issues created by digital transformation

text: These issues have not yet risen to the forefront because of the cost and inconvenience involved in accessing justice system data. However, establishing a data-driven justice system may require re-thinking what and how information is collected and stored and the best approaches to ensuring data quality, availability and accessibility (see Box 1). Addressing issues of data quality and coverage becomes even more important in the context of artificial intelligence (AI) in justice systems. The example of AI underscores the need for guardrails in data governance frameworks to manage the potential risks associated with AI systems, ensuring the objectives and values for people-centred justice are preserved.

text:
 11

Support data sharing within and beyond the formal justice system

New models of governance are also needed to support data sharing among actors within, and agencies outside, the formal justice system. The PCJ Framework recognises that, in general, when attempting to resolve their justice issues, people rarely reach the stage of involving institutions of the formal justice system. Indeed, across countries, only 11% of respondents with justiciable problems have recourse to formal justice institutions, and only another 4% to other processes, including mediation and arbitration (OECD/Open Society Foundations, 2019[8]).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça
metadata.section_path: Support data sharing within and beyond the formal justice system

text: Most people’s justice journeys start and end before they ever reach a court or tribunal. Previous OECD assessments suggest that people’s pathways of action for dispute resolution outside of courts often involve the police, lawyers, professional legal organisations, online advice services, legal aid offices, doctors, pharmacists, schoolteachers, family, friends, and acquaintances (OECD, 2024[9]). As such, delivering people-centred justice requires policymakers and justice actors to have access to data that are collected, stored and managed by a diverse range of stakeholders outside the formal justice system (see Box 2).

text:
12 

Delivering people-centred justice may require actors to share, link and re-use data that have been provided for another purpose. This encompasses, for example, combining data held by justice system agencies and service providers for the purposes of research (e.g. linking administrative records from health with data from justice systems and services). This helps to gather better information on who uses services and to identify opportunities to intervene earlier (see Box 3). Relevant data may be held by private actors, such as insurance companies, who may be unwilling to share data for commercial reasons. Concerns about client confidentiality, legal professional privilege and the independence of the legal profession may mitigate against law firms and legal advice agencies sharing data about the experience of their clients. Therefore, these approaches may test the “social license” for data use (see Box 3).

text:
 13

Create mechanisms to ensure that justice data governance itself reflects the PCJ Framework

To date, existing justice data governance frameworks tend to privilege the views, experience and perspectives of justice system actors and professional users in decisions about data collection, sharing and use. A people-centred justice approach to data governance models is therefore essential to enable the justice system to meet people’s legal and justice needs.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: According to the PCJ Framework, people-centricity refers to a human-centred approach that adopts the perspective of people as a starting point. This involves placing people at the core when designing, delivering, monitoring and evaluating public policies, services and legal procedures within and beyond the justice system. It takes into account the perspectives and needs of specific communities, including marginalised and underserved groups, and groups in vulnerable situations (e.g. women, children, indigenous groups, the elderly and people with disabilities) (OECD, 2023[1]). Taking the needs and voices of people into account entails, at a minimum, undertaking consultation and research to understand people, including their needs and interests (Lopez Solano et al., 2022[13]) (OECD, 2021[10]) (see Box 4).

text:
Beyond investing in research, consultation and participatory decision-making models, data governance for people-centred justice must also create mechanisms to support people and communities to contest particular uses of data, hold actors accountable and secure redress (see Box 6).

Effective data governance for meaningful accountability must recognise that data collection and use affect collectives and the public, not just individuals. Accordingly, effective data governance supports institutional, as well as individual responses to data production and exploitation. Secondly, effective data governance enables the identification of problems and claims for redress at different stages of a data-driven intervention or application, not just at the initial approval stage. Thirdly, effective data governance can support the development of legal, structural and institutional mechanisms that empower people to dissent from, or not consent to, a given application or use of data (Lopez Solano et al., 2022[13]). In this way, effective data governance serves to equalise the power differentials around data interventions.

text: As in the justice sector, the health sector is another example where robust, context appropriate, privacy protective health data governance frameworks are needed to preserve public interests, trust and bring significant benefits to individuals and society. Recognising this, the OECD Recommendation on Health Data Governance is an important tool to guide countries in setting the framework conditions for enabling the availability and use of personal health data to unlock its potential. It also provides a roadmap towards more harmonised approaches to health data governance across countries (see Box 7).

text:  17 Objectives and values of data2 governance for people-centred justice Context At a minimum, data governance must ensure that fundamental rights are upheld, and that existing laws and regulations are complied with. However, to be truly effective, data governance must also sustain the social license for data use (see Box 3). In this regard, justice data governance frameworks must enable clear articulation of the objectives that the collection, sharing and use of data aims to achieve, and the values that programmes and projects produce. From the PCJ Framework, two major objectives for justice data governance can be defined. Effective justice data governance for people-centred justice should enable the collection, use, management and sharing of data to: 1. Understand people’s needs and experiences with legal and justice services from their perspective; and 2. Develop and implement policies and services that meet those needs and remove barriers to access as part of a holistic vision for a people-centred justice ecosystem.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: ices from their perspective; and 2. Develop and implement policies and services that meet those needs and remove barriers to access as part of a holistic vision for a people-centred justice ecosystem. Projects and programmes relating to the collection, storage, sharing, use and maintenance of justice data should be assessed according to their potential to advance these objectives. The following discussion expands on these objectives and describes the kinds of projects that serve to advance them, with examples of initiatives and good practices. Achieving the objectives in practice Understanding people’s needs and experiences with legal and justice services from their perspective Understanding people’s legal needs from their perspective, whether they recognise that these needs are legal or not, is critical to the design and delivery of services that address unmet needs. Data on when, where and how problems are experienced, and by whom, are critical to the delivery of people-centred justice. Administrative data that are collected by legal systems and services (e.g.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: s. Data on when, where and how problems are experienced, and by whom, are critical to the delivery of people-centred justice. Administrative data that are collected by legal systems and services (e.g. courts, ombuds, law firms, legal aid providers, community advice services) reveals only a fraction of the actual legal needs of the population. This type of data source only captures the characteristics and experiences of those people who manage to access existing services. Therefore, governments should also look to gather data on those who cannot or do not access justice services.

18 

Governments should therefore consider investing in projects to collect data about the needs and experiences of people who do not reach the formal legal system, and who may not even realise that the problem they are experiencing could benefit from a legal solution. Investment to facilitate this type of data collection is key to designing policies and services that expand access to justice and address unmet needs.

text: The kinds of initiatives that may be developed to advance this objective vary in novelty and complexity. Legal Needs Surveys are a popular tool among policymakers to gather data on how people experience their legal needs (see Box 8). They provide an empirical basis for understanding how peoples’ justice issues arise and are experienced, therefore contributing to a broad range of development priorities (OECD/Open Society Foundations, 2019[8]). The OECD/Open Society Foundations report on Legal Needs Surveys and Access to Justice sets out a framework for the design, implementation and analysis of Legal Needs Surveys. It provides modular tools that can be applied in different types of surveys and examines the concepts, framing, scope and units of measurement used in Legal Needs Surveys.

text:
However, sample sizes from Legal Needs Surveys are rarely large enough to support small areas or local mapping of needs (OECD/Open Society Foundations, 2019[8]). Accordingly, there is increasing interest in projects that apply insights from Legal Needs Surveys to official datasets and administrative datasets (such as the National Census data, social security data, and crime data) (OECD, 2021[2]).

While many of the datasets relevant to understanding legal needs are collected and held by wider government agencies, private companies may also hold and collect some of the most useful data for delivering people-centred justice. These data are usually generated as a by-product of activities unrelated to law and justice (Lopez Solano et al., 2022[13]).

For example, in one study, researchers used anonymised mobile phone data to predict the incidence of domestic violence at a neighbourhood level. In the context of the ongoing ubiquity of help seeking on social media platforms and websites, academics in the United States have developed machine learning tools to support the identification of unidentified and unmet legal needs from user generated content submitted to Reddit (see Box 9).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
 19

Projects that involve the re-use of data provided in a context unrelated to law and justice are more likely to test the social license for data use. This is particularly the case when data to identify and understand legal needs are re-used in a way that threatens the contextual integrity of the underlying data (see Box 9).

text: Accordingly, when designing, considering, assessing or deploying initiatives that involve the re-use of data, it is recommended that decision makers adopt a responsible approach to data re-use. This encompasses having a clear and well-defined purpose for data re-use, prioritising what benefits all people (see Box 10). As part of this responsible approach, practitioners should capture and communicate the origin, potential biases, limitations, and previous uses of datasets to ensure that those reusing the data are clear on what insights the data can and cannot provide. While recognising that risks can never be fully erased, practitioners should ensure an adequate level of data aggregation to guard against group privacy harms and re-identification of individuals (GovLab, 2020[19]). Adopting a transparent communication strategy and engaging with local communities and actors, data stewards and trusted intermediaries can help ensure not only quality and accuracy, but also ethical and responsible use of data (see Box 10).

text:
Developing and implementing policies and services as part of a holistic people-centred justice ecosystem

Supporting the design of policies and services that meet people’s needs is fundamental to deliver people- centred justice. Developing strong data governance frameworks that support the combination of data required to understand the legal needs of people with other data held by actors both in and outside the justice system is necessary to achieve this aim.

Analysing data about people’s needs can help identify gaps in existing policies and services where interventions may be required. This information must be representative, covering diverse groups of people and their interaction with legal and justice services.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: In addition to legal needs surveys, data held in court records, such as judgments and transcripts, can also be important sources. These data can support the development of a more detailed understanding of people’s experience of the formal legal system, and the extent to which the system is meeting their needs. Given the widely recognised asymmetries in power and knowledge between people delivering justice services and those in receipt of them, data capable of supporting objective and expert assessments of the performance of justice processes is critical to ensure that services meet people’s needs. This type of data can be gathered from court observations and court documents, including hearing transcripts and judgments.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: For example, in 2022, the Ministry of Justice in the United Kingdom conducted research into the experience of victims of domestic violence in the family courts in England and Wales. The research combined data from a range of sources, including literature reviews, focus groups and an analysis of existing judgments and decisions. The final report identified serious and persistent issues with the way in which the courts treat victims of domestic violence in private family law cases (Government of the United Kingdom, 2023[20]). The report led to the development of proposals for a data-driven oversight mechanism to monitor and improve the experience of victims of domestic abuse across the family courts. To this end, it calls to create

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
 21

a network of expert court observers to monitor the treatment of allegations of domestic abuse by the judiciary.

Linking user satisfaction data to administrative data can enable stakeholders to understand whether particular groups of people are more or less satisfied with their experience using legal and justice services. As such, combining user satisfaction data and administrative data can produce valuable insights to design services that meet people’s needs on an equal basis. Box 11 illustrates an example of using national surveys, a case management system, and administrative data to target interventions to improve the performance of Access to Justice Centres in Argentina.

text:
Data can also support the effective development of user-centred and legal design strategies. User research, a key component of user-centred design and digital transformation activities, is a powerful technique that has supported the creation of many digital services. Despite its benefits, user research can also sample an inadequate number of cases or individuals, leading to services that do not address the needs of all users. Box 12 illustrates an example where the lack of a sufficiently representative sample of cases and users resulted in the development of digital services that underperformed for people in vulnerable situations.

Quantitative and representative data covering the full range of cases and people who use (or are intended to use) legal services and systems offer an outlook of legal needs across the whole population. It is therefore important to provide policy and service design teams with access to representative data. This can counterbalance the risk of sampling bias associated with in-depth qualitative research techniques often used in more granular design activities.

text: Designing services and policies that meet people’s needs requires policy makers to invest in tools to capture users’ subjective perceptions of the performance of services. In the context of court processes and other dispute resolution processes, it is essential to measure users’ perceptions of the procedural justice of services and systems. Perceptions of procedural fairness are key to people’s willingness to accept decisions, even when the outcome is not in their favour. In addition, perceptions of procedural justice have been found to be linked to public trust and confidence in legal authorities and institutions (Tyler, T., 2001[23]).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: Instruments have been produced to assess procedural justice from the perspective of users. Particularly in North America, they have been tested in a wide range of settings, including experimental and survey work (MacCoun, 2005[24]). A number of court leaders in the US are currently using such instruments with the support of the Centre for Justice Innovation, a not-for-profit research organisation (Center for Justice Innovation, 2015[25]). In British Columbia, the Civil Resolution Tribunal has introduced a user satisfaction survey with questions that map procedural justice to understand the extent to which the tribunal is meeting people’s expectations (Government of Canada, 2023[26]). While efforts to run satisfaction surveys have been conducted in jurisdictions in Canada and the US, it is worth mentioning that this remains an exceptional practice on the global scale.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
Finally, teams designing policies and services also require access to data from outside the justice system to ensure that those policies and services meet people’s needs. For example, the ability to link data about people’s experience of the justice system and justice outcomes, to data in health or education records, can help governments to design better policies and devise new approaches to delivering justice services. The United Kingdom has linked data from the Ministry of Justice, the Department of Health and Social Care, and the Department of Levelling Up, Housing and Communities, to understand which services are most effective in preventing prison leavers from becoming homeless, and what role drug treatment services can play in preventing homelessness (Government of the United Kingdom, 2022[27]).

Strong data governance within the justice system is required so that the people and organisations holding that data have sufficient trust to provide access. Efforts are required to create appropriate capacity,

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
 23

regulation and data infrastructure to ensure that data are used for the purpose of delivering people-centred justice services and systems. These topics are covered in Chapter 3.

text:
Upholding the values of the people-centred justice framework

In addition to ensuring that data initiatives contribute to achieving the objectives identified above (see Achieving the objectives in practice in Chapter 2), it is important that the values of the people-centred justice framework are promoted and guaranteed. The aims of projects that collect, share, use and maintain data, and the way these projects are conducted, should uphold and align with the values that underpin the people-centred justice framework.

Three values that are foundational to a people-centred justice culture include: (1) a commitment to equality; (2) judicial independence; and (3) maintaining and enhancing public trust in justice systems. The following sections provide an overview of these values and their implications for data governance in justice systems.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça
metadata.section_path: Upholding the values of the people-centred justice framework

text:
Equality

A key tenet of the OECD Recommendation on Access to Justice and People-Centred Justice Systems is promoting equal access to justice for all (OECD, 2023[1]). The PCJ Framework recognises that justice systems exist in a context of unevenly patterned need and disadvantage. It advocates for the design of legal and justice services to actively overcome the barriers access to justice by providing the assistance that people need (OECD, 2021[2]). In adopting this approach, the PCJ Framework advocates for justice systems to commit to a vision of equality that is substantive, rather than formal in nature.

A commitment to substantive equality has implications for both the types of data related to projects to be prioritised, and the conditions that are imposed on these projects as they develop. For example, when assessing whether to prioritise investment in a particular project, policy makers must consider who will benefit from the project, and whether the benefits of the project will be distributed to those who are most in need (see Box 13).

text:
Judicial independence

Judicial independence is recognised under national and international laws as an essential feature of effective justice systems and critical to the maintenance of the rule of law. The PCJ Framework explicitly recognises judicial independence as foundational to the delivery of people-centred justice (OECD, 2021[2]).

Judicial independence requires the judiciary to be free from any external pressures, including political influence or manipulation. An independent judiciary is one where judges are free to make impartial decisions solely on fact and law. As such, judicial independence is best understood not as an end in itself, but a means of ensuring that judges are free to decide cases impartially (Venice Commission, 2010[33]; UNODC, 2020[34]; OSCE, 2009[35]).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: In recent years, the growing recognition of the potential for detailed data about court processes, court actors and case outcomes to be collected and shared has prompted debate about the ways in which these data could undermine judicial independence. For example, data on court judgments could promote practices by the Executive branch to analyse judicial decision-making patterns in order to monitor or discipline judges who depart from the norm (CEPEJ, 2018[36]). Likewise, the collection, aggregation and publication of information on judicial decision-making might result in the creation of “norms by majority trend”. Judges themselves may be reluctant to deviate from such norms, undermining vitality in judicial interpretation (ECHR, 2016[37]). In addition, concerns have been raised about the impact of the increased data mining of justice on opportunities to game the system. One example includes forum shopping, where parties choose to withdraw, adjourn or transfer cases to a judge that they consider more likely to provide them with a favourable outcome (CEPEJ, 2018[36]).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
Recognition of the potential for data practices to undermine judicial independence is found in the European Union (EU) General Data Protection Regulation 2016 (GDPR), and in the EU AI Act. Under GDPR, courts and tribunals, when acting judicially, are excluded from the competence of supervisory bodies to preserve judicial independence (Custers et al., 2022[38]). Data held by courts is excluded from Freedom of Information legislation in some common law jurisdictions (e.g. England and Wales).

At present, there remains little empirical evidence to prove or disprove the impact of collecting and publishing data about judicial decisions on judicial independence (Townend, J. and Wiener, C., 2021[5]). The impact of changes to the way in which data are published and used on judicial independence may vary from country to country due to wider political and social factors. As such, when considering whether to prioritise and pursue data projects and programmes, decision makers should identify any risks in relation to judicial independence and take steps to mitigate them. Decision makers may also want to consider

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:  25 implementing mechanisms to monitor the impact of changes to data collection, sharing and use of judicial data on judicial independence. Public trust The imperative to rebuild trust between institutions and the people they serve is identified as a key driver of the transition to people-centred justice (OECD, 2021[2]). However, where not well designed nor implemented, projects and programmes that seek to collect, share, maintain and use data can undermine public trust in both data driven initiatives and the institutions who deliver them (Grimmelikhuijsen, 2015[39]). There is a growing body of good practices which aims to support policy makers to design, develop and implement data collection, sharing and use in a way that commands public trust (OECD, 2021[10]). A number of good practice steps can be identified from research in data-driven health. To build and maintain public trust, policy makers could consider ensuring that any project or programme focuses solely on collecting, using and sharing data that are necessary to achieve its objectives. This emphasises the importance of minimalism in data handling practices.

metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: hat any project or programme focuses solely on collecting, using and sharing data that are necessary to achieve its objectives. This emphasises the importance of minimalism in data handling practices. Another key step is to evaluate any proposed initiative against insights gleaned from comprehensive research involving stakeholders and the public. This process helps to comprehend and pinpoint potential risks concerning public trust, guiding decisions towards more informed and transparent practices. For example, the LEF-funded research on public attitudes towards court data re-use in the United Kingdom (see Box 3) identified specific concerns about the availability of witness names in employment tribunals. Therefore, initiatives proposing to make these data more widely available carry additional risks to public trust and require further scrutiny. Creating a clear, straightforward explanation of the project's goals, the data to be utilised, the project leaders and foreseeable risks becomes integral.

Creating a clear, straightforward explanation of the project's goals, the data to be utilised, the project leaders and foreseeable risks becomes integral. Clear communication acts as a foundation for engaging with stakeholders and the public, promoting transparency and comprehension (see Support data sharing between and beyond the formal justice systems in Chapter 1). Before initiating any data sharing activities, it is necessary to publicly announce the project. To promote openness and allow public input from the outset, publicly announcing the project should include details on how and where stakeholders and the public can express dissent. It is equally important to enable these dissent mechanisms throughout the project's duration. Providing avenues for dissent allows continuous public engagement and ensures their voices are heard. Lastly, establishing a monitoring framework to gauge shifts in public attitudes over time serves as an ongoing evaluation tool. This continuous assessment helps in adapting strategies to maintain and bolster public trust throughout the project lifecycle.

Applying the objectives and values in practice Effective data governance frameworks regulate for participation by different actors in decision making about data. They allow for negotiations between competing stakeholders and interests and provide ways in which conflicts can be mediated and resolved. Table 2 shows how the framework of objectives and values described in this chapter can be used to guide discussions and decision making. The answers to the questions should be recorded in the documentation of the decision and made publicly available, alongside information about how to engage with or dissent from the project, and routes for redress. text:  27 Applying the OECD model for data3 governance to the justice sector The OECD model for Data Governance Approaches to public sector data governance may vary in focus. Some may emphasise technical governance aspects, while others underline specific data governance elements that are available but dispersed. To address these different needs, the OECD proposes a holistic model for data governance in the public sector. It is intended to bring greater clarity and structure to the definition and implementation of data governance across countries. The OECD model is based on extensive OECD work on digital government and data. It has been used to analyse progress across a range of countries, including the series of the OECD Digital Government Review. The OECD model for data governance explores key features of governance needed to support the delivery of a data-driven public sector. It includes six dimensions, which can be divided into three layers: strategic, tactical and delivery (OECD, 2019[40]) (see Figure 1). These three layers are mutually reinforcing to attain a sound data governance ecosystem (van Ooijen, Ubaldi and Welby, 2019[41]). Figure 1.

text:
28 

Strategic layer

Leadership and vision

Strong leadership that embraces a clear vision of data-driven justice is an essential feature of all successful data governance frameworks. The OECD has identified that strong leadership is crucial to ensure strategic direction and purpose, and to create clear accountability both for progress and for fidelity to goals of data governance (OECD, 2019[40]). These goals align with the aims and principles outlined in Objectives and values of data governance for people-centred justice in Chapter 2.

To this end, it is essential for leadership to develop a common vision for justice across society; the systemic indicators to support decision making in line with this vision; and the data required for justice services to be designed and delivered in line with the system’s goals. This provides a foundation to guide subsequent data governance decisions and implementation. Likewise, leadership requires coordinating actors across the public and private sector at a national or sectoral level.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
Strong leadership is particularly important in the specific context of justice data governance. Justice data are held across a complicated network of public and private actors, each with their own incentives, systems, culture, policies and practices. Arrangements for collecting, storing, sharing and publishing justice data in many jurisdictions tend to evolve over time to support the delivery of particular functions or business models. As such, arrangements for collecting, storing, linking, sharing and using justice data are complex, inconsistent and fragmented in many jurisdictions.

Understanding people’s justice pathways is key to harnessing justice data. This requires an understanding of the ways in which people interact with, and move between, organisational and institutional boundaries, and across justice services and systems. This requires aligning data policies and practices across actors and negotiating constitutional sensitivities.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
While these challenges are particularly acute in the justice space, they are far from unique. Data governance frameworks to harness data to improve health outcomes, for example, face similar challenges. The experience of implementing data governance for health is instructive in identifying the types of leadership that is needed to support data use in the justice space. These include defined political and judicial leadership, responsibility and accountability specified in legislation and clear data strategies.

Political and judicial leadership

Identifying the specific actors who should hold responsibility for, and demonstrate leadership over, justice data can be complex. This is often due to the constitutional and legal issues that are potentially implicated in the sharing and linking of data across the different branches of government. In practice, joint leadership between the judiciary and executive, as part of a shared strategic approach for the role of justice data, is preferable to leadership that is vested in any one branch of government. Moreover, such a hybrid approach is more likely to lead to better outcomes and more sustainable change (see Box 14).

text:
Data strategies

Data strategies are an important element of good data governance. They can enable accountability within the systems being governed and help define leadership, roles, expectations and goals (OECD, 2019[40]).

There are many examples of data strategies for elements of the justice sector, with several provided as case studies within this paper. These are typically for state-delivered elements of the justice sector. However, at present, there remains a lack of good practices that comprehensively encompass a people- centred justice system. This would include people-centred policies and services, public and private actors, data to understand the scope and impact of justice problems, and data holders that are inside and outside of the justice system. Previous data strategies, and the lessons learnt from delivering them, provide helpful resources in creating new people-centred justice data strategies.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
There are a large range of stakeholders involved in delivering people-centred justice. As people-centred justice data strategies are developed, political and judicial leaders will need to be clear on the value of data governance and the objectives that it must adhere to. At the same time, leadership must be aware that the strategy is setting a new direction for data governance across this landscape and that justice stakeholders need to both align with the strategy and help realise it in practice. As such, developing new data strategies requires strong, carefully designed and meaningful stakeholder engagement and consultation. This approach should enable inputs from a wide-ranging group of stakeholders and consider their perspectives throughout the development process.

Legislation

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: Enshrining the objectives and values of justice data governance in legislation can be an effective mechanism for ensuring accountability and sustainability in data governance. For example, in the United Kingdom, provisions to facilitate the sharing of patient data are set out in primary legislation. This legal framework enables the Secretary of State for Health to make regulations to support the sharing of data “in the interests of improving patient care or in the public interest” (NHS, 2016[46]). This type of legislation can have positive knock-on effects on the governance of justice and non-justice data, which is stewarded by public, private or third sector organisations. Countries will need to ensure that there are appropriate

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
30 

legislative and regulatory safeguards against misuse of the data or the misuse of the powers over that data (e.g. by current political leadership or by individual organisations). This requires effective democratic scrutiny and appeal mechanisms.

Placing the rationale for data sharing in legislation helps to ensure ongoing alignment with the objectives and values of data governance. Similarly, demarcating the person(s) responsible for leading data governance in statute creates clear lines of accountability. This clarity and certainty can help support actors across the private and public sectors to more effectively engage in data collection, sharing and re-use (see Box 15).

text:
Tactical layer

Capacity for coherent implementation

Successful policy implementation relies on the intersection of different factors. These can range from the establishment of inter-institutional coordination bodies grounded in adequate institutional networks, to capacity-building initiatives, collaboration and knowledge sharing (OECD, 2019[40]).

The following sections highlight the role that inter-institutional coordination bodies can play in supporting actors across the justice system to collect, use, share and maintain justice data. It examines how this can contribute to the delivery of people-centred justice systems and services that are accessible, effective, equitable, and transparent. It also highlights good practices and examples of existing coordination bodies (OECD, 2019[40]).

Inter-institutional coordination bodies

Inter-institutional bodies are often responsible for advising on budget priorities for data management and use. They may also be charged with ensuring that data strategies and projects take a risk management approach, in order to anticipate and respond to policy challenges as they emerge.

text:
Building institutional and organisational capacity

In addition to political and judicial leadership, investment in administrative leadership and capacity is important to deliver effective governance for justice data. The OECD report “The Path to Becoming a Data- Driven Public Sector” explores effective approaches to driving digital transformation across the public sector, highlighting that the importance of these roles goes beyond mere technical aspects (OECD, 2019[40]).

In other areas of social policy, investing in institutional and organisational capacity to collect, store, use and share data is crucial for harnessing the benefits of data to improve broader outcomes across society. In addition to capacity building in terms skills and research, organisations are creating new roles and responsibilities and appointing ambassadors for data use in the justice sector. This helps to drive forward progress on harnessing data to deliver strategic priorities (ADR UK, 2023[52]).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
32 

In England and Wales, His Majesty’s Courts and Tribunals Service has created a new role entitled “Head of Data Access”. This position supports the delivery of goals set out by their organisational data strategy. Likewise, in the United States, the Utah Judicial Council (i.e. the administrative arm of the state courts) announced the creation of a new “Office for Fairness and Accountability”. The Office is dedicated to tackling racism and bias. As such, the Office Director is mandated to “work with lawmakers and the executive branch to gather data, reach out to marginalised groups, and train and recruit court employees”. Additionally, in the United States, the Legal Services Corporation is investing in a fellowship scheme to provide not-for-profit recipients of its funding with the capacity and skills to collect, use and share data to improve organisational effectiveness and increase access to justice (Knox, 2020[53]).

Data stewardship

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
Data stewardship is the act of using, collecting and managing data within an organisation. Each organisation within the people-centred justice system is making data stewardship decisions within the context of the broader data governance framework and their own organisational objectives.

A large range of data stewardship models are currently being used at either a national, sectoral, or organisational level. These models are often referred to as data intermediaries, data governance or data institutions. They can co-exist within a justice system, or as a specific data value chain within a justice system.

However, these existing approaches to data stewardship have limitations. Existing regulation to protect people from harm caused by data-related activities is often insufficient, and could better harness the benefits of data-related activities. There is also limited consensus on how to best balance the trade-offs between drawbacks (i.e. insufficient protection against harm versus the inadequate support for the creation of benefits), how to transition to new models, and the role of new regulatory frameworks versus self- regulated operational practices.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
A range of practical and academic actors are exploring how to improve existing models, and how to create new types of stewardship models (e.g. data cooperatives and trusts). This forms part of broader efforts to understand the contexts in which these models are useful, and to make recommendations on which regulatory and institutional frameworks would help scale-up existing models. As each model has different purposes, values and primary beneficiaries, they can have differing modes of accountability. For example, a data trust provides some forms of accountability through fiduciary duties and regulations.

A study commissioned by the European Parliament identifies the dominant conceptual bases that underpin most existing data stewardship models. The study argues that most existing frameworks conceive of data as a strategic national asset or as a proprietary asset (i.e. belonging to those who use and manage it) with limited restrictions for personal data (Lopez Solano et al., 2022[13]). It highlights the emergence of six different data stewardship models that represent alternatives to this dominant approach (see Box 17).

text:
Regulation

A people-centred justice system operates within an environment of cross-cutting and sectoral regulation. The regulatory entities are a mix of state bodies and non-state bodies (e.g. data protection regulators and professional associations for lawyers).

One of the roles of the leadership function is to ensure that these regulatory entities have the capability, capacity and lines of accountability to help deliver on the goals of the justice data framework. As such, both the regulatory entities and their regulatory frameworks must be easily understandable and accessible to justice stakeholders.

However, this regulatory landscape is constantly evolving. New cross-cutting regulation is emerging around data and AI, which may have a future impact on justice data governance. Likewise, regulatory gaps remain around issues like algorithmic accountability (ALI, 2021[54]) and AI harms (AWO, 2023[55]), while

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
34 

new types of systems – such as large language models (LLMs) – are emerging and are likely to require ongoing changes to legal and regulatory frameworks.

Cross-cutting regulation

The primary cross-cutting regulatory focus of data governance is usually seen as data protection, but a range of other cross-cutting regulations also apply to data-related activities. Data protection legislation creates data protection authorities (DPAs) that are mandated to enforce legislation in their jurisdiction. These DPAs also have regulatory authority over the justice sector.

Data protection law has a long history, starting with the OECD Guidelines on the Protection of Privacy and Transborder Flows of Personal Data in 1980, followed by the Council of Europe’s Convention for the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data (CETS No. 108) in 1981. Data protection legislation was originally designed to protect the privacy of individual citizens against the state.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: The focus has latest shifted towards providing individual rights for the protection of personal data, while promoting the free flow of personal data for economic and state purposes (Edwards, 2019[56]). More recent examples of data protection legislation include the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) adopted in 2016. In many data protection legal frameworks, justice data are considered highly sensitive for individuals (e.g. Article 10 of GDPR on the processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences). Research conducted as part of a public deliberation exercise suggests that people consider information in court records to be as sensitive as the information held in medical records (see Box 4). If the data have been published under the requirement of anonymisation, it might be important to consider regulation that can protect individuals from associated risks, such as re-identification.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
Alongside data protection, other forms of cross-cutting regulation also apply to data-related activities and the organisations that perform them. This includes human rights, anti-discrimination and equality regulations, and health and safety, labour rights and administrative law. It may also include professional standards (e.g. attorney client privilege).

More recently, governments are creating new cross-cutting regulations focused on parts of the economy and society that have been created or grown in scale and/or importance. These new regulations may affect certain activities within a people-centred justice system (see Box 18).

text:
Sectoral regulation

As with many parts of society and the economy, there are pre-existing sectoral regulations and regulators within the justice sector. The duties, responsibilities, powers and tools of many regulators in other sectors have been updated for reasons including: the changes brought about by the digital transformation; the opportunities of digitalisation for new services; and the risks that digital transformation and increased use of data entails for both users and broader society. These risks might emerge through the interactions between people and new services, or changes to how existing services are delivered through the use of data driven approaches (Diver and McBride, 2022[60]).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: A tension between supporting innovation and preventing new harms can often surface in debates about sectoral regulation. For example, precautionary behaviour based on potential harms has been underlined as unnecessarily reducing innovation. To help navigate these tensions, new approaches to regulation are being developed and proposed (e.g. anticipatory regulation), though their effectiveness in practice has not been evaluated (Nesta, 2019[61]). In this regard, it is important that countries view these tensions as a way of simultaneously tackling harms and supporting opportunities. The objectives and values for data governance in a people-centred justice system should closely guide this work.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: It is not yet clear what future sectoral regulation may be required for the use of data within justice systems by Legaltech services. However, any data governance framework adopted for justice data should include robust monitoring and evaluation frameworks and implement controls and safeguards around data use. Justice sector leadership should be validating that relevant sectoral regulators have these capabilities. This must include robust lines of accountability, accessible mechanisms for redress in the case of harm, and

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
36 

could include accreditation of products and services to demonstrate that they meet national standards (AWO, 2023[55]).

At present, very few sectors have well-established practices to seize the opportunities of the digital age. Due to the limited number of established practices for seizing sectoral opportunities, people-centred justice systems may need to debate, test and implement new practices. This should be accompanied by capacity building efforts among justice regulators to develop and enforce these practices.

Typically, finance and healthcare are seen as successful in seizing sectoral opportunities. For instance, open banking initiatives indicate one way to support the design of new policies and services that meet people’s needs (see Box 19).

text:
Delivery layer

The delivery layer encompasses the processes, mechanisms and tools facilitating the practical implementation of data governance at a granular level (OECD, 2019[40]).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
 37

Data value chain

The data value chain can be understood as a sequence of activities through which data are collected, processed, analysed, and used to generate value (van Ooijen, Ubaldi and Welby, 2019[41]). This value can be economic, social or organisational.

The data value chain is a cyclical process. The model presented in Box 20 helps trace the journey from handling raw, isolated and unstructured datasets, to recognising and understanding relationships within the data, and then transforming them into information and knowledge. This knowledge serves as a foundation to make strategic, tactical or operational decisions and take action.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: Acknowledging the diversity of stakeholders in a people-centred justice system, both within and outside the public sector, the justice data value chain is similarly composed of multiple organisations collecting, storing, sharing and using data. Given the global and segmented nature of digital and data markets, some of these organisations are likely to exist in different legal jurisdictions. The data value chain operates across this federated system. Strong strategic and tactical layers in the data value chain reinforce the delivery layer, contributing to attaining the desired objectives and values of a people-centred justice system (see Achieving the objectives in practice and Upholding the values of the people-centred justice framework in Chapter 2).
