metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
Generating and collecting

Data held or used within a people-centred justice system is generated by human or natural activity and captured by some entity (see Table 1), meaning that there is no such thing as raw data (Gitelman L., 2013[66]). As the starting point for the application of data within government, it is important to recognise that the data accessed by public servants can take many forms and come from multiple sources. A person or organisation capturing data may have had particular purposes or processes that, intentionally or not, affect how the data are recorded, what it is useful for, and what impact the act of generation and capture may have had on people and communities. As such, it is fundamental to consider the data source to ensure that the data are suitable for use, but also that they have been captured in a way that meets the desired objectives and values of a people-centred justice system. For example, data that have been captured illegally should never be used in any justice system. However, data may be sourced from an exchange that is produced by another data value chain.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: tice system. For example, data that have been captured illegally should never be used in any justice system. However, data may be sourced from an exchange that is produced by another data value chain. Likewise, data from an exchange may be purchased as a dataset, provided as part of an analytics service, or made freely available.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
While the sources for these data might be within the people-centred justice system, sources can also exist within non-justice sectors which may require more critical examination. For example, some sources of statistical justice data may be designed to meet the needs of government decision makers rather than non- state actors. Similarly, some sources of data about individuals may not have an appropriate form of consent or social license to be used (see Box 4 and Box 5).

In relation to justice data on individuals, consent should be conceived through the individual lens provided by data protection law (i.e. where consent is typically only one acceptable legal basis) but also as the act of ensuring an acceptable basis for data capture. This acceptable basis can include both individual permission/consent and the types of societal or community consent that may be provided through a formal democratic and legal process or a participatory method (Ridpath J., 2022[67]). The basis should be both legally and ethically acceptable to the impacted individuals or communities.

Storing, securing and processing

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
Once data are identified, collected and generated, data are then transmitted to some form of storage and validated to understand what it is useful for. The act of storage may involve multiple organisations. This is particularly the case as processing moves into the domain of the private sector, with cloud service providers often using a mix of open and proprietary software.

At an early point in the government data value cycle, it is important to focus on producing good quality data to support its re-use. Data quality assessments, and potentially cleansing activity, form part of validation for data re-use. While good quality data is optimal, it is also important to recognise that quality can mean different things to different data users. For instance, a longitudinal research project can use statistical techniques to handle uncertainty in data, while an arbitration service provider needs a high level of confidence in the identity of the individuals that it is serving.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:  39 Documenting, understanding and communicating quality to data users is an important first step to preserve trust in the management of data and organisations that hold them. A number of approaches to understanding and communicating data quality and other information about datasets are being adopted in different parts of the data ecosystem. Some examples are datasheets for datasets, within the AI/ML community and data quality dimensions within the United Kingdom (Gebru et al., 2018[68]) (UK DQH, 2021[69]). In addition to these approaches, security infrastructure needs to be treated as a high priority topic (see Manage the opportunities and issues created by digital transformation in Chapter 1; and Box 10). Sharing, curating and publishing At this stage – when data are being shared, curated and published – the potential impacts of using data are no longer limited internally to the public sector. Instead, they begin to reach those external to government who can begin to use shared data. Legislation and infrastructure can affect how easily requests for access and data sharing agreements are managed for data that are not publicly available.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: government who can begin to use shared data. Legislation and infrastructure can affect how easily requests for access and data sharing agreements are managed for data that are not publicly available. When there are explicit efforts to support data sharing, curating and publication, the public sector should focus on the early stages of the cycle in prioritising interoperability platforms and licensing, ensuring high data quality (OECD, 2019[40]). Using and re-using The final step in the data value chain is the use and re-use of data. This step includes both packaging the data into something useable by an end user and the act of trading the insights (GSMA, 2018[70]). Data might be packaged into a report alongside other insights and analysis, presented as data visualisation, or used to deliver another service (e.g. legal advice). The packaging may allow users to further process and analyse the data themselves. The packaging process is increasingly likely to allow the end user to scrutinise the chain of events that led to the insight. This process contributes to promote transparency as it allows the end user to scrutinise the chain of events that led to the insight.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: nd user to scrutinise the chain of events that led to the insight. This process contributes to promote transparency as it allows the end user to scrutinise the chain of events that led to the insight. Ultimately, this also contributes to trust in data use and re-use. The packaging process might require transparency about how the data were captured, information about the quality of the data, and an explanation of how the analysis was performed. The level of scrutiny may vary according to legal requirements and different users’ needs. The trading takes place through several mechanisms. If a data value chain produces a data output (e.g. market insights about demand for particular types of legal services), the outputs might be published in the public domain or made available for a fee on a data marketplace. If a data value chain produces more transactional or advisory services, then the data outputs may be made available at commercial advice centres or through tribunals and courts. Data infrastructure Data infrastructure includes: • Registers - authoritative lists that people can trust; • Catalogues and discoverability - ways for users to find data;

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: through tribunals and courts. Data infrastructure Data infrastructure includes: • Registers - authoritative lists that people can trust; • Catalogues and discoverability - ways for users to find data; • Platforms - shared APIs, research repositories, and identity systems; and • Data services - providing data as an ongoing service to users. Each of these elements could be applied as digital public infrastructure – sometimes called a digital public good (Lopez Solano et al., 2022[13]; DPGA, 2022[71]) – as well as a range of other business models. In line with trends in other sectors, digital public infrastructure is likely to expand overtime to encompass more elements. This provides a sustainable baseline for services and research, while encouraging and supporting innovation in more emergent and novel spaces. As data infrastructure evolves and expands,

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: 40  business model decisions should be made within the overall context of national justice systems and uphold the objectives and values of people-centred justice (see Objectives and values of data governance for people-centred justice in Chapter 2). Registers Registers are authoritative lists that people can trust (Downey, 2015[72]). They make it easier for people and organisations to use data by providing strong, foundational building blocks from which to build services or perform analysis. Within a people-centred justice system, registers might include: • Criminal court locations; • Registered justice service providers; • Lists of registered professionals (e.g. judges, solicitors, mediators); • A list of justice cases; or • A list of algorithms used in the justice system. For centuries, registers have been administered by institutions such as professional membership bodies (see Box 21), mapping agencies, and registrars of companies or regulated service providers. These institutions have become trusted through a combination of longevity, the quality of the services they provide, and the governance mechanisms that have been built around them, such as statutory duties around

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: utions have become trusted through a combination of longevity, the quality of the services they provide, and the governance mechanisms that have been built around them, such as statutory duties around accountability. In more recent decades, many of these existing institutions have digitised the data in the lists they steward, using architectural practices such as standards and APIs. This has required an update of associated statutory duties around digital publishing and new use cases. These could include an expectation to provide a list of algorithms used to ensure transparency. A people-centred justice system similarly creates the need for new registers and accompanying institutions. Debate and experimentation are required to arrive at decisions on the level of access of datasets, such as records from alternative dispute resolution pathways. Box 21. Poland: The national register of mediators The National Register of Mediators is part of the project "Dissemination of alternative dispute resolution methods by increasing the competences of mediators, establishing the National Register of Mediators and information activities", implemented by the Polish Ministry of Justice and

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: ve dispute resolution methods by increasing the competences of mediators, establishing the National Register of Mediators and information activities", implemented by the Polish Ministry of Justice and financed by the European Social Fund. The National Register of Mediators serves as a public register that is transparent and available to everyone. It contains information on mediators conducting in-court and out-of-court mediations. The Register has an online functionality that allows all users to search for an appropriate mediator via its website. The Register also includes a catalogue of mediator names, specialisations and categories of cases for mediation. The system also serves as a referral tool for both common court judges and mediators, enhancing collaboration and a seamless pathway between litigation and mediation services. The planned functionalities of the system enable court cases to be referred to mediation through the system and allow the circulation of documents such as case files, mediation protocols and draft mediation settlements. Source: Government of Poland (2024[73]), National register of mediators.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:  41 Discoverability Discoverability is a long-standing need within any form of digital governance. While data might be made available, it must also be discoverable so that people can use it. Discoverability is therefore an important consideration when designing and delivering efficient and people-centred justice services. Discoverability has evolved alongside digital tools from early portals and search engines, to more sophisticated tools such as recommendation algorithms. Within the field of data governance, tools are being developed for people who experience justice issues and cases, researchers who analyse them, and public and private sector innovators who create justice services. The creation of these tools is enabled by standardised metadata that describe datasets, who can use them and what they are useful for. For instance, a data catalogue can be a fundamental tool for ensuring discoverability and clarity of data and related services. In addition, standards to underpin these tools are emerging, such as the European Case Law Identifier (ECLI).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: a fundamental tool for ensuring discoverability and clarity of data and related services. In addition, standards to underpin these tools are emerging, such as the European Case Law Identifier (ECLI). Platforms The term “platform” is used in the generic sense in this section to refer to any shared API, shared component, identity system (Pope, 2019[74]) or shared research data repository which are used to access data. Platforms might include: • APIs that exchange bulk open data between organisations, that exchange personal data between trusted organizations with the consent of a data subject, or that provide a single verified credential about an individual (W3C, 2022[75]). • Shared components might include data storage systems, data visualisation tools, data sharing platforms or performance dashboards that show the performance of multiple organisations and services within a system. • Identity platforms are often the most challenging and riskiest to build and govern. Verifying someone’s identity is essential to providing many rights and services, but identity is also one of the most sensitive attributes of individuals and can be one of the hardest to prove at a distance through a

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: e’s identity is essential to providing many rights and services, but identity is also one of the most sensitive attributes of individuals and can be one of the hardest to prove at a distance through a digital service. • Shared research repositories bring together data from various sources and make it available for research, analysis or product/service development (SAIL, 2023[76]) (ONS, 2023[77]). Some research repositories are moving to more federated models, rather than a single platform. Platforms help to deliver the data value chain and can form part of the infrastructure that supports a peoplecentred justice system. A growing number of governments are using platform strategies to deliver on digital government goals and to help deliver public sector digital justice services, such as submitting a case to a tribunal or applying for a court order. This can increase the efficiency and scale of data, and support broader efforts to make public services more accessible and inclusive. A growing number of governments are using platform strategies to deliver on digital government goals for these reasons.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: d support broader efforts to make public services more accessible and inclusive. A growing number of governments are using platform strategies to deliver on digital government goals for these reasons. In a digital context, platforms are best developed based on some indication of user and organisational needs. Yet, they need to be further adopted to be truly useful as platforms rather than as a point solution for a single use case or organisation. A platform might be shared by multiple business units within a single organisation or by multiple organisations. It needs to find a business model and funding that supports its usage and ensures that the platform remains operational and useful. Widely shared and used platforms hold significant power to influence and shape how data are, and can, be used. To this end, it is particularly important that their governance (e.g. decisions about who can use them or what features they support) is aligned with the objectives and values of people-centred justice. Data about the performance of platforms should be publicly available. This helps users decide which platform to use and support accountability.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: ith the objectives and values of people-centred justice. Data about the performance of platforms should be publicly available. This helps users decide which platform to use and support accountability. The performance data should be verifiable and auditable and

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: 42  should provide an appropriate breakdown of performance for different users and justice use cases. The performance breakdown should allow civil society to verify that the platform conforms with relevant legislation (e.g. anti-discrimination, justice sector-specific). The impact of platforms should be independently evaluated on a regular basis to validate that their use remains consistent with the desired outcomes of people-centred justice. Given the importance of public trust in a people-centred justice system, it is essential to find an approach to identity that suits the local context. A range of business models for platforms exist, including: • Free platforms, funded by the state and provided as public infrastructure (e.g. a national identity system, or a platform for applying for a court order); • Free to self-host, the software for the platform is available for free as open-source code, but users need to pay the operational costs for hosting and supporting it; • Pay-per-use, users pay a fee based on units of usage. For example, a data processing API which charges € 0.01/1000 uses above a certain free level;

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: e operational costs for hosting and supporting it; • Pay-per-use, users pay a fee based on units of usage. For example, a data processing API which charges € 0.01/1000 uses above a certain free level; • Pay-per-commercial use, users pay a fee based on usage for commercial, revenue-generating purposes. For example, a data processing API which charges € 0.02/1000 uses above a certain free level to for-profit justice service but offers the same service for free to not-for-profit justice services; or • Pay-for access, where users pay a recurring fee for access to the platform. Data services The provision of data (e.g. official statistics, performance or transparency data) is increasingly designed in the same way as digital services. Approaches such as user-centred design (UCD) and the use of multidisciplinary teams are widely applied in service design and applied when data are seen as a service (e.g. open data portals, APIs, data marketplaces data analytics services). Thinking of data as a service also brings a recognition that the provision of data is often an ongoing, iterative task rather than a one-off activity. However, this approach also presents several risks.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: inking of data as a service also brings a recognition that the provision of data is often an ongoing, iterative task rather than a one-off activity. However, this approach also presents several risks. As UCD methodologies have been developed in large commercial organisations, they can lead to an excessive focus on individual service users at the expense of the broader network of stakeholders (Mani-Kandt et al, 2021[78]). As many of the impacts and risks of data are borne by non-data users, this means that UCD approaches need to be combined with a broad definition of users, coupled with systems thinking and participatory approaches that look for and mitigate potential adverse consequences (Jones, 2014[79]; Tonkinwise C; Degl'Innocenti F, 2021[80]; Design Council, 2022[81]). Supporting data practitioners to develop communities of practice, playbooks and guides for how to build data services responsibly in a way aligned with people-centred justice will help navigate these risks and bring desired benefits. Data architecture Within data architecture, this working paper considers standards and interoperability.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: aligned with people-centred justice will help navigate these risks and bring desired benefits. Data architecture Within data architecture, this working paper considers standards and interoperability. Standards make it easier for organisations to publish, access, share and use quality data. They can be used to provide a consistent definition of what counts as a completed court case, or how to describe the demographics of a witness. Standards need to be developed in an inclusive way that supports desired outcomes and leads to their adoption. Institutions can have an important role in supporting the development of standards in a collaborative and inclusive way. Interoperability is based on standards. It refers, for example, to sharing information on a court case between two trustworthy legal service providers. Interoperability supports data analysis and research, and enables justice system users to move between or change service providers. In other sectors, regulators

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:  43 are mandating service interoperability to increase competition between private sector service providers in digital markets. Standards Standards can be described as reusable agreements that make it easier for people and organisations to publish, access, share and use better quality data (Open Data Institute, 2018[82]). Technical standards have long been recognised as useful mechanisms to make tasks repeatable by many people, to create outputs that can be shared between many organisations, and to make it easier for organisations to switch between standardised components (e.g. data models, APIs, security mechanisms). Technical standards can support and embody goals such as competition, interoperability, equality and safety. Standards for data are no different. In recognition of their benefits, the OECD OURdata Index measures adoption and use of standards as part of government efforts to ensure the availability, accessibility and re-usability of government data (OECD, 2019[40]). The Global Data Barometer, an initiative of Open Data for Development and ILDA, also measures adoption and use of technical standards as one of its indicators for good data governance (Global Data

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: ]). The Global Data Barometer, an initiative of Open Data for Development and ILDA, also measures adoption and use of technical standards as one of its indicators for good data governance (Global Data Barometer, 2022[83]). Within a people-centred justice system, a standard might describe a number of different types of data and processes. For example: • The location and accessibility of court buildings; • How a case is defined and what makes it complete; • Mechanisms for exchanging case data between justice professionals or service providers; • Design patterns for collecting demographic information about justice system users; • How to report performance data to regulators; • A framework for measuring justice outcomes; • A framework for measuring justice experiences (Armstrong et al., 2020[84]). Some of these standards might be specific to the justice sector (e.g. types of cases, area of law, professions), while others might be used in multiple sectors (e.g. location of buildings or design patterns for collecting demographic information). While standards have many benefits, they also come with risks. For example:

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: rs might be used in multiple sectors (e.g. location of buildings or design patterns for collecting demographic information). While standards have many benefits, they also come with risks. For example: • Standards development processes may not be inclusive and support participation from all groups. This can lead to standards that do not support the needs of all actual and potential users of the justice system; • Standards development processes can move too slowly to adapt to evolving technological possibilities, and human and societal needs; • Standards documentation can be costly or be published under restrictive licenses, presenting unfair limitations on how it can be used; • Mandatory standards may be difficult to adopt and impose compliance costs that unnecessarily reduce the objectives of the justice system being met; • Unnecessary threats to commercial interests can lead to standards processes becoming highly contested, with associated legal costs and court cases; • The task of turning human activity into a specified data format risks losing some of the nuanced human experiences.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: processes becoming highly contested, with associated legal costs and court cases; • The task of turning human activity into a specified data format risks losing some of the nuanced human experiences. These risks have led to standards processes becoming more formal, with a need to demonstrate that due process has been followed, and more open, to support greater participation and adaptability. In parallel with these trends, there is an increasing recognition that standards should not be seen as solely a technical

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: 44  matter. Instead, they should be seen as part of broader policy development with a wide range of skills and voices involved in their development (OECD, 2019[40]). To manage these opportunities and risks, countries could carefully consider: • Processes and institutions for standards development; • Recommendations on standards adoption; and • Support for standards adoption. Existing national and global standards development organisations (SDOs) (e.g. the W3C, IEEE and ISO), can provide foundations for standards development. Justice sector experts would need to participate in the processes of standards development. Within particular jurisdictions, organisations may develop their own standards, but should follow good practices such as the OpenStand principles (IEEE, 2014[85]). Within a people-centred justice system, funding may be needed to support participation in standards processes, particularly for organisations that represent people who may be most at risk of harm from increased data use or unfair justice outcomes.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: may be needed to support participation in standards processes, particularly for organisations that represent people who may be most at risk of harm from increased data use or unfair justice outcomes. It is also important for countries to consider standards adoption, including how and when organisations should be required to use a standard and what support might be provided. Organisations can be mandated or required to use a standard (i.e. where the standards are de jure) to operate in a particular section of the justice system where the standard is already being broadly applied (i.e. de facto standards). Decisions on mandating standards adoption are akin to a regulatory function and require implementation by institutions with a formal role, responsibility and process. Decisions on standards adoption may be split across multiple institutions or left to the market. For example, a public sector organisation may determine mandatory standards for criminal court services. Additionally, a regulator may set mandatory standards for performance data.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: left to the market. For example, a public sector organisation may determine mandatory standards for criminal court services. Additionally, a regulator may set mandatory standards for performance data. In some cases, a multi-stakeholder body, authorised by the regulator, may decide when a standard for transferring case data between service providers should become mandatory. Similarly, the market may adopt a de facto standard for describing justice services. A support function to assist organisations to incorporate standards into their processes and systems is an important part of a data governance framework, yet is frequently overlooked. Mechanisms to accelerate the adoption of standards across a sector can support the attainment of overarching people-centred justice policy goals and can realise the potential benefits of the data standard. Support mechanisms can include standards catalogues and roadmaps to help people discover standards; guides; conversion tools; compliance validation tools; business cases; or access to funding and expertise. Interoperability Interoperability is a mechanism for computing systems to work together (Brown, 2021[86]).

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: rsion tools; compliance validation tools; business cases; or access to funding and expertise. Interoperability Interoperability is a mechanism for computing systems to work together (Brown, 2021[86]). It can include both data and service interoperability for the purposes of: • Data analysis and research, for example to understand the efficacy of justice services for people with differing demographic characteristics; • Supporting justice service providers’ needs to communicate information with each other, for example by disclosing legally required case information; or • Supporting people’s needs to move between legal advisors, service providers or justice pathways, for example by allowing them to easily move their whole case file from a mediation centre to a court system. Within a people-centred justice system, each of these purposes could involve both public and/or non-public justice service providers. Interoperability can provide great benefits. For example, it can help combine datasets from multiple systems for research or make it easier for a litigant to change their legal advisor if the service they receive

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text:
 45

is unsatisfactory. However, interoperability can also come with risks. For example, an insecure interoperability architecture could lead to data breaches that damage public trust, while a poorly designed interoperability architecture may unfairly benefit some justice service providers over others.

Interoperability between the public and private sectors and within the private sector is, in most cases, less advanced than other public sector initiatives. This is generally seen to result from a limited alignment of incentives between competing organisations. This misalignment is an issue to which people-centred justice systems need to pay particular attention. Interoperable Europe, an initiative led by the European Commission and adopted by the Council of the EU, aims to enhance collaboration and information exchange among member states in justice and home affairs. Box 22 provides more details on the key elements of this framework.

text: 46  Conclusion4 This working paper explores the critical role of data governance in delivering people-centred justice. It provides a comprehensive examination of the values, objectives and practices necessary for effective data governance in justice systems. It takes as a starting point OECD policy tools, including the OECD Framework and Good Practice Principles for People-Centred Justice and the OECD Data Governance Framework, and sets the ground for future research on data governance in justice. The exploration of data governance for people-centred justice outlined in this paper highlights the critical role that data can play in modernising justice systems. Drawing from comprehensive desk research, stakeholders’ interviews, and the OECD’s various frameworks and recommendations, the paper underscores the necessity for effective data governance to ensure justice systems are responsive to the needs of people. Recognising the need for effective data governance and that delivering people-centred justice requires a cultural shift in the way justice services and systems are designed and delivered, new justice data governance frameworks are needed to support a transition to

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: vering people-centred justice requires a cultural shift in the way justice services and systems are designed and delivered, new justice data governance frameworks are needed to support a transition to people-centred justice. In particular, policy makers should consider new frameworks that re-orientate data collection practices from recording data solely relevant to the agencies to data that helps understand the pathways, experiences and needs of the people who seek to navigate the justice system. New justice data governance frameworks should also consider constitutional/legal concerns on data collection, sharing and use, as well as opportunities and challenges associated with digital transformation. To date, existing justice data governance frameworks tend to privilege the views, experience and perspectives of justice system actors and professional users in decisions about data collection, sharing and use. This working paper also encourages the adoption of a people-centred justice approach to data governance models to enable the justice system to meet people’s legal and justice needs.

metadata.title: Towards effective governance of justice data
metadata.author: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: , sharing and use. This working paper also encourages the adoption of a people-centred justice approach to data governance models to enable the justice system to meet people’s legal and justice needs. In addition, this working paper encourages the adoption of governance mechanisms that support data sharing between actors within and beyond and agencies outside the formal justice system. Effective justice data governance for people-centred justice should enable the collection, use, management and sharing of data in view of two major objectives: first, understanding people’s needs and experiences with legal and justice services from their perspective; and second, developing and implementing policies and services that meet those needs and removing barriers to access as part of a holistic vision for a people-centred justice ecosystem. This working paper introduces the application of the OECD model for data governance to the justice sector. It intends to support policy makers in designing new data governance models for people-centred justice. The model encompasses three layers – strategic, tactical and delivery –, mutually reinforcing to achieve a sound data governance.

metadata.theme: Governança de dados de justiça

text: rs in designing new data governance models for people-centred justice. The model encompasses three layers – strategic, tactical and delivery –, mutually reinforcing to achieve a sound data governance. In particular, as part of their new models for data governance policy makers should consider: • Strong leadership that embraces a clear vision of data driven justice; • Capacity for coherent implementation, including inter-institutional coordination bodies grounded in adequate institutional networks, capacity-building initiatives, collaboration and knowledge sharing; • Regulatory functions that have the capability, capacity and lines of accountability to help deliver on the goals of the justice data framework; and • Processes, mechanisms and tools facilitating the practical implementation of data governance at a granular level.

text: viii Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health. Guidance on large multi-modal models Executive summary Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to the capability of algorithms integrated into systems and tools to learn from data so that they can perform automated tasks without explicit programming of every step by a human. Generative AI is a category of AI techniques in which algorithms are trained on data sets that can be used to generate new content, such as text, images or video. This guidance addresses one type of generative AI, large multi-modal models (LMMs), which can accept one or more type of data input and generate diverse outputs that are not limited to the type of data fed into the algorithm. It has been predicted that LMMs will have wide use and application in health care, scientific research, public health and drug development. LMMs are also known as “general-purpose foundation models”, although it is not yet proven whether LMMs can accomplish a wide range of tasks and purposes. LMMs have been adopted faster than any consumer application in history.

text: eneral-purpose foundation models”, although it is not yet proven whether LMMs can accomplish a wide range of tasks and purposes. LMMs have been adopted faster than any consumer application in history. They are compelling because they facilitate human–computer interaction to mimic human communication and to generate responses to queries or data inputs that may appear human-like and authoritative. With rapid consumer adoption and uptake and in view of its potential to disrupt core social services and economic sectors, many large technology companies, start-ups and governments are investing in and competing to guide the development of generative AI. In 2021, WHO published comprehensive guidance (1) on the ethics and governance of AI for health. WHO consulted 20 leading experts in AI, who identified both potential benefits and potential risks of use of AI in health care and issued six principles arrived at by consensus for consideration in the policies and practices of governments, developers, and providers that are using AI.

text: tential risks of use of AI in health care and issued six principles arrived at by consensus for consideration in the policies and practices of governments, developers, and providers that are using AI. The principles should guide the development and deployment of AI in health care by a wide range of stakeholders, including governments, public sector agencies, researchers, companies and implementers. The principles are: (1) protect autonomy; (2) promote human well-being, human safety and the public interest; (3) ensure transparency, “explainability” and intelligibility; (4) foster responsibility and accountability; (5) ensure inclusiveness and equity; and (6) promote AI that is responsive and sustainable (Figure 1). WHO is issuing this guidance to assist Member States in mapping the benefits and challenges associated with use of LMMs for health and in developing policies and practices for appropriate development, provision and use. The guidance includes recommendations for governance, within companies, by governments and through international collaboration, aligned with the guiding principles.

Ethics and governance of LMMs in health care and medicine LMMs can be considered products of a series (or chain) of decisions on programming and product development by one or more actors (Figure 2). Decisions made at each stage of an AI value chain may have both direct and indirect consequences on those who participate in the development, deployment and use of LMMs downstream. The decisions can be influenced and regulated by governments by enacting and enforcing laws and policies nationally, regionally and globally.

One way of framing the governance of LMMs is in the three stages of the AI value chain: (i) the design and development of general-purpose foundation models or LMMs; (ii) provision of a service, application or product based on a general-purpose foundation model; and (iii) deployment of a health-care service or application. In this guidance, each phase is examined with respect to three areas of enquiry: • What risks (described above) should be addressed at each stage of the value chain, and which actors are best placed to address those risks? • What can a relevant actor do to address the risks, and which ethical principles must be upheld? • What is the role of government, including relevant laws, policies and regulations? Certain risks can be addressed at each phase of the AI value chain, and certain actors are likely to play more important roles in mitigating each risk and upholding ethical values.

Liability for LMMs As LMMs gain broader use in health care and medicine, errors, misuse and ultimately harm to individuals are inevitable. Therefore, liability rules might ensure that users harmed by an LMM are adequately compensated or have other forms of redress to both reduce the burden of proof by a user who is harmed, ensuring that such individuals are adequately and fairly compensated. Governments can do so by introducing a presumption of causality. They might also consider introducing a strict liability standard for any harm that results from deployment of an LMM. Although strict liability rules may ensure compensation for those who suffer harm, they may also discourage use of increasingly sophisticated LMMs. Governments might also consider no-fault, no-liability compensation funds.

text: 1 Introduction 1 1 Introduction This guidance addresses the emerging uses of large multi-modal models (LMMs) for healthrelated applications.2 It includes the potential benefits and risks of use of LMMs in health care and medicine and approaches to the governance of LMMs that could best ensure compliance with guidelines and obligations for ethics, human rights and safety. The guidance builds on WHO guidance issued in June 2021 – Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health (1), which addressed the ethical challenges and risks of use of artificial intelligence (AI) in health, identified six principles for ensuring that AI is used to the public benefit of all countries, and issued recommendations to enhance the governance of AI for health in order to maximize the promise of the technology. AI refers to the capability of algorithms integrated into systems and tools to learn from data to perform automated tasks, without programming of each step explicitly by a human. Generative AI is a category of AI techniques in which machine learning models are used to train algorithms on data sets to create new outputs, such as text, images, videos and music.

metadata.title: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health. Guidance on large multi-modal models
metadata.author: World Health Organization (WHO)
metadata.theme: Ética e governança de grandes modelos multimodais aplicados à saúde

text: citly by a human. Generative AI is a category of AI techniques in which machine learning models are used to train algorithms on data sets to create new outputs, such as text, images, videos and music. Generative AI models learn patterns and structures from training data and produce new data based on predictions made from the learnt patterns. Generative AI models can be improved by reinforcement learning with human feedback, wherein human trainers rank responses provided by generative AI models to train algorithms to issue responses that maximize how much humans will value the response. Generative AI has potential applications in various fields, including design, content generation, simulation and scientific discovery. Much attention has been focused on a specific type of generative AI, large language models, which receive one type of input – text – and provide a response that is also in text. Large language models are examples of large unimodal models, which are the basis for the operation of early versions of chatbots that integrate these models. Although large language models engage in dialogue, the models themselves have no conception of what they are producing.

Therefore, LMMs can accept more than one type of input and generate outputs that are not limited to the type of data entered. LMMs are envisioned for diverse applications in health care and drug development. LMMs differ from previous types of AI and machine learning. Another difference between LMMs and other forms of AI is their versatility. Previous and existing AI models, including for medical uses, are designed for specific tasks and are therefore inflexible. They can execute only tasks defined in the training set and its labels (5) and cannot adapt or carry out other functions without retraining with a different dataset. Thus, even though more than 500 AI models for clinical medicine have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration in the USA (5), most are approved for only one or two narrow tasks. In contrast, LMMs are trained on various datasets and can be used in numerous tasks, including some for which they were not explicitly trained (5). LMMs usually have an interface and format that facilitate human–computer algorithm interactions that might mimic human communication and which can therefore lead users to imbue the algorithm with human-like

text: sually have an interface and format that facilitate human–computer algorithm interactions that might mimic human communication and which can therefore lead users to imbue the algorithm with human-like qualities. Thus, the way in which LMMs are used and the content they generate and provide as responses, which may appear to be “human-like”, are different from those of other forms of AI and have contributed to the unprecedented public adoption of LMMs. Furthermore, because the responses they provide appear to be authoritative, many users uncritically accept them as correct, even if an LMM cannot guarantee a correct response and cannot integrate ethical norms or moral reasoning into the responses it generates. While this guidance illustrates the different ways in which LMMs are used (or imagined for use) in health care and medicine, they are already used in numerous domains, including education, finance, communications and computer science. LMMs can be considered products of a series (or chain) of decisions on programming and product development by one or more actors.

LMMs can be considered products of a series (or chain) of decisions on programming and product development by one or more actors. Decisions made at each stage of an AI value chain may have both direct and indirect consequences on those that participate in the development, deployment and use of LMMs downstream. The decisions can be influenced and regulated by governments that enact and enforce laws and policies nationally, regionally and globally. The AI value chain often begins in a large technology company. The developer could also be a university, a small technology company, a national health system, public-private consortiums or other entities that have the resources and capacity to use several inputs, which comprise “AI infrastructure”, such as data, computing power and AI expertise, to develop generalpurpose foundation models. These models can be used directly by a user to perform various, often unanticipated tasks (including those related to health care). Several general-purpose foundation models are trained specifically for use in health care and medicine.

A general-purpose foundation model can be used by a third party (a “provider”) through an active programming interface for a specific purpose or use. This involves (i) fine-tuning a new LMM, which may require additional training of the foundation model; (ii) integrating the LMM into applications or a larger software system to provide a service to users; or (iii) integrating components known as “plug-ins” to channel, filter and organize the LMMs into formal or regulated formats to generate “digestible” results.3 3 Communication from Leong Tze-Yun, WHO expert on the ethics and governance of AI for health.

The customer who acquires or licenses the product or application may then use it directly for patients, health-care providers, other entities in the health system or laypeople or in its own business. The value chain can be “vertically integrated”, so that a company (or other entity, such as a health system) that collects data and trains a general-purpose foundation model can modify the LMM for a particular use and provide the application directly to users. WHO recognizes the tremendous benefits that AI could provide to health systems, including improving public health and achieving universal health coverage. Yet, as described in the WHO guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health (1), it entails significant risks that could both undermine public health and imperil individual dignity, privacy and human rights.

Even though LMMs are relatively new, the speed of their uptake and diffusion led WHO to provide this guidance to ensure that they could potentially be used successfully and sustainably worldwide. WHO recognizes that this guidance is being issued at a time of many competing views about the potential benefits and risks of AI, the ethical principles that should apply to its design and use and approaches to governance and regulation. As the guidance is being issued shortly after the first applications of LMMs in health care and before successively more powerful models will be released, WHO will update the guidance to keep up with the rapid evolution of the technology, how society addresses its use and the health consequences of the use of LMMs beyond health care and medicine. 1.1 Significance of LMMs LMMs, although relatively new and untested, have had an inordinate impact on society in various domains, including health care and medicine.

Chat GPT, a large-language model, successive versions of which have been released by a US technology company, was estimated to have 100 million monthly active users in January 2023, just 2 months after its launch. At the time, this made it the fastest-growing consumer application in history (6). New companies, backed by millions of US dollars in private investment, are developing competing LMMs (9). Open-source LMMs are also emerging more quickly and inexpensively than those developed by the largest companies, due to the availability of such platforms (10). One study found that, while one large language model, GPT-3, “in comparison to humans… can product accurate information that is easier to understand”, it can also produce “more compelling disinformation”, and humans cannot distinguish content generated by the LMM from that generated by a human (16). Governments have also been largely unprepared. Regulations and laws written to govern the use of AI may not be fit to address either the challenges or opportunities associated with LMMs. The European Union, which has reached an agreement to enact an European Union-wide Artificial Intelligence Act, had to revise its legislative framework in the final stages of drafting to account for LMMs (17). Other governments are rapidly developing new laws or regulations (18) or have instituted temporary bans (several of which have already been rescinded) (19).

The challenges, principles and recommendations were the basis for the expert group’s approach to LMMs presented in this guidance. Box 1. Brief overview of WHO consensus ethical principles for use of AI for health • Protect autonomy: Humans should remain in control of health-care systems and medical decisions. Providers have the information necessary to use AI systems safely and effectively. People understand the role that AI systems play in their care. Data privacy and confidentiality are protected by valid informed consent through appropriate legal frameworks for data protection. • Promote human well-being, human safety and the public interest: Designers of AI satisfy regulatory requirements for safety, accuracy and efficacy for well-defined uses or indications. Measures of quality control in practice and quality improvement in the use of AI over time should be available. AI is not used if it results in mental or physical harm that could be avoided by use of an alternative practice or approach. • Ensure transparency, “explainability” and intelligibility:

text: be available. AI is not used if it results in mental or physical harm that could be avoided by use of an alternative practice or approach. • Ensure transparency, “explainability” and intelligibility: AI technologies should be intelligible or understandable to developers, medical professions, patients, users and regulators. Sufficient information is published or documented before the design or deployment of AI, and the information facilitates meaningful public consultation and debate on how the AI is designed and how it should or should not be used. AI is explainable according to the capacity of those to whom it is explained. • Foster responsibility and accountability to ensure that AI is used under appropriate conditions and by appropriately trained people. Patients and clinicians evaluate development and deployment of AI. Regulatory principles are applied upstream and downstream of the algorithm by establishing points of human supervision. Appropriate mechanisms are available for questioning and for redress for individuals and groups that are adversely affected by decisions based on AI. • Ensure inclusiveness and equity:

Appropriate mechanisms are available for questioning and for redress for individuals and groups that are adversely affected by decisions based on AI. • Ensure inclusiveness and equity: AI is designed and shared to encourage the widest possible, appropriate, equitable use and access, irrespective of age, sex, gender identity, income, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation, ability or other characteristics. AI is available for use not only in high-income settings but also in lowand middle-income countries. AI does not encode biases to the disadvantage of identifiable groups. AI minimizes inevitable disparities in power. AI is monitored and evaluated to identify disproportionate effects on specific groups of people. • Promote AI that is responsive and sustainable: AI technologies are consistent with the wider promotion of the sustainability of health systems, the environment and workplaces.

Guidance on large multi-modal models 2 Applications and challenges of use of LMMs in health Applications of AI for health include diagnosis, clinical care, research, drug development, health-care administration, public health and surveillance. Many applications of LMMs are not novel uses of AI; however, clinicians, patients, laypeople and health-care professionals and workers access and use LMMs differently. This section addresses the potential applications of LMMs in health care and the actual and expected challenges and risks associated with its use. Many applications and uses are still unproven and may ultimately not deliver the benefits that have been advertised. 2.1 Diagnosis and clinical care AI is already used in diagnosis and clinical care, for instance to assist diagnosis in fields such as radiology and medical imaging, tuberculosis and oncology. It had been hoped that clinicians could use AI to integrate patient records during consultation, to identify at-risk patients and as an aid in difficult treatment decisions and to catch clinical errors (1).

text: been hoped that clinicians could use AI to integrate patient records during consultation, to identify at-risk patients and as an aid in difficult treatment decisions and to catch clinical errors (1). LMMs could make it possible to extend use of AI-based systems throughout diagnosis and clinical care – both virtual and in-person consultations, with some experts expecting that LMMs “will be more important to doctors than the stethoscope in the past” (20). Several LMMs have passed the US medical licensing examination; however, passing a written medical test by regurgitating medical knowledge is not the same as providing safe, effective clinical services (21), and LMMs have failed tests with material not previously published online or that could be easily solved by children (22). One study of the clinical knowledge of a large language model concluded that “transitioning from a large language model that is used for answering medical questions to a tool that can be used by healthcare providers, administrators, and consumers will require considerable additional research to ensure the safety, reliability, efficacy and privacy of the technology” (23).

Diagnosis is seen as a particularly promising area, because LMMs could be used to identify rare diagnoses or “unusual presentations” in complex cases (24). Doctors are already using Internet search engines, online resources and differential diagnosis generators, and LMMs would be an additional instrument for diagnosis. LMMs could also be used in routine diagnosis, to provide doctors with an additional opinion to ensure that obvious diagnoses are not ignored. All this can be done quickly, partly because an LMM can scan a patient’s full medical record much more quickly than can doctors (24). Several popular LMMs now being used in pilot programmes to support clinicians were not, however, trained specifically on electronic health records or medical or other relevant health

For example, in several health-care systems in the USA, an LMM provided by one technology company is being pilot-tested to read messages from patients and to draft responses from doctors to reduce the time that medical staff spend in replying to patient queries. This practice is intended to decrease the burn-out of health-care workers, who field thousands of messages daily, and to enable them to focus on their clinical duties (“keyboard liberation”) (25). Thus, when a patient message is received, the LMM displays a draft reply based on both information from the patient and a version of their electronic medical history. While the AI is used only for some patient questions, the replies require heavy editing (25). Nevertheless, a study in the USA found that a Chat GPT-powered chatbot performed better than qualified doctors in responding to questions posed on an online forum. Of the 195 questions selected, independent evaluators preferred the chatbot responses to the physician responses in nearly 80% of cases (26).

Of the 195 questions selected, independent evaluators preferred the chatbot responses to the physician responses in nearly 80% of cases (26). Chatbots should also be helpful in answering standardized “curb-side consult” questions and providing information and responses on the initial presentation of a patient or to summarize laboratory test results (27). Companies and universities are also developing LMMs trained with medical and health data or electronic health records, which include LMMs based on small data sets. For example, one LMM was trained on a dataset of an estimated 30 000 medical case reports to learn the relations between medical conditions and symptoms to assist in diagnoses (28). Another LMM was trained on a dataset of over 100 000 chest X-rays to identify abnormalities and eventually provide insights or identify conditions (29). Several LMMs that have been publicly evaluated were trained with an algorithm on millions of electronic health records and other sources of specialized and general medical knowledge.

The approach improved the ability of an algorithm to process different forms of written medical information and to issue responses (“medical question answering”) (30). Several of the largest technology companies are adapting their general-purpose LMMs to ones that could assist in clinical diagnoses and care. One technology company is developing MedPaLM 2, which is intended to answer questions and summarize insights from medical texts and is now evolving to synthesize images (such as X-rays and mammograms) to write reports and respond to follow-up questions, to facilitate additional queries by clinicians, a functionality that could mitigate “peer disagreement” between a health-care worker and a computer (31). The long-term vision is to develop “generalist medical artificial intelligence”, which will allow health-care workers to dialogue flexibly with an LMM to generate responses according to customized, clinician-driven queries.

text: 10 Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health. Guidance on large multi-modal models Risks of use of LMMs in diagnosis and clinical care The promise of LMMs in clinical care is accompanied by significant risks associated with their use, several of which predate LMMs. Five major risks have been identified of use of LMMs in diagnosis and clinical care. • Inaccurate, incomplete, biased or false responses: One concern with respect to LMMs has been the propensity of chatbots to produce incorrect or wholly false responses from data or information (such as references) “invented” by the LMM (32) and responses that are biased in ways that replicate flaws encoded in training data (33). LMMs could also contribute to contextual bias, in which assumptions about where an AI technology is used result in recommendations for a different setting (1). For example, there is under-representation of training data and perspectives from lowand middle-income countries. Thus, if an LMM is asked to summarize a treatment paradigm for a disease to guide a ministry of health in a low-income country, it might reproduce an approach that is appropriate only for a high-income context (34).

metadata.title: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health. Guidance on large multi-modal models
metadata.author: World Health Organization (WHO)
metadata.theme: Ética e governança de grandes modelos multimodais aplicados à saúde

text: is asked to summarize a treatment paradigm for a disease to guide a ministry of health in a low-income country, it might reproduce an approach that is appropriate only for a high-income context (34). Furthermore, an LMM may provide an incomplete answer, no response at all or a response that does not account for changed circumstances in the setting in which it is being used. False responses, known colloquially as “hallucinations”, are indistinguishable from factually accurate responses generated by an LMM, because even LMMs with reinforcement learning from human feedback are not trained to produce facts but to produce information that looks like facts. One study found that large language models, when provided a simple set of facts to summarize, would hallucinate at least 3 percent of the time and as high as 27 percent (35). Current LMMs also depend on human “prompt engineering”, in which an input is optimized to communicate effectively with an LMM (36). Thus, LMMs, even if trained specifically on medical data and health information, may not necessarily produce correct responses.

text: which an input is optimized to communicate effectively with an LMM (36). Thus, LMMs, even if trained specifically on medical data and health information, may not necessarily produce correct responses. For certain LMM-based diagnoses, there may be no confirmatory test or other means to verify its accuracy (24). In medicine and other areas of public health decision-making, use of LMMs, even if they are factually correct most of the time, may not be accurate enough to justify the cost of developing them or the cost of implementing them in health-care systems safely and effectively. • Data quality and data bias: One reason that LMMs produce biased or inaccurate responses is poor data quality. Many of the LMMs currently available for public use were trained on large datasets, such as on the Internet, which may be rife with misinformation and bias. Most medical and health data are also biased, whether by race, ethnicity, ancestry, sex, gender identity or age. LMMs trained on health data often encode such biases, as most data are collected in high-income settings. For example, genetic data tend to be collected disproportionately on people of European descent (1).

Problems of data quality and bias affect all AI models, including LMMs (1).

text: 2 Applications and challenges of use of LMMs in health 11 Box 2. Ethical considerations for the use of LMMs by children While broad guidance has recently been published for safe, ethical use of paediatric data in AI and machine learning (ACCEPT-AI) (43), special consideration must be given to the potential impacts of use of LMMs by children. The wide availability of open LMMs provides access by users of various ages. There is, however, limited evidence on how children engage with or use LMMs. While the potential opportunities and drawbacks of LMM use have been discussed in wider educational contexts (44), it is unclear how such engagement by children affects their mental or physical well-being. Their use of LMMs must be monitored over time to understand the benefits and potential harms. Laws and policies on paediatric consent, assent and stipulations for legal parental involvement differ among and within countries. Thus, lack of cohesive, unified, global, child-specific regulation and oversight could result in unidentified, unmonitored harm, especially from use of LMMs. Specifically, it is not clear how accurately LMMs generalize paediatric health.

metadata.title: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health. Guidance on large multi-modal models
metadata.author: World Health Organization (WHO)
metadata.theme: Ética e governança de grandes modelos multimodais aplicados à saúde

text: al, child-specific regulation and oversight could result in unidentified, unmonitored harm, especially from use of LMMs. Specifically, it is not clear how accurately LMMs generalize paediatric health. Studies have shown that generalization of adult data sets to the paediatric population may be limited. Paediatric data should therefore be kept separate in testing and training datasets (45). Developers should include demographic information on training data that includes age and must be encouraged to provide clear descriptors of target populations, including age ranges, for appropriate, safe engagement with LMMs, as relevant. When legally possible, LMMs should be improved by including appropriate engagement and feedback from young users. One technology company states on the system card for its LMM (GPT-4): “We found that GPT-4-early and GPT-4-launch exhibit many of the same limitations as earlier language models, such as producing biased and unreliable content” (37). LMMs can be limited by the end date of data with which the algorithm was trained, although some LMMs can now access up-to-date information from the Internet.

LMMs can be limited by the end date of data with which the algorithm was trained, although some LMMs can now access up-to-date information from the Internet. For example, Chat GPT-4 was trained on data up to September 2021 (38) but can now search or browse the Internet for up-to-date information (39). This could, however, lead to generation of more false or inaccurate information. The previous “end-date” prevented introduction of false newly published material (39). In medicine, both up-to-date and highly accurate information is critical for meeting standards of care as well as for understanding certain diseases. • Automation bias: Concern that LMMs generate false, inaccurate or biased responses is heightened by the fact that, as with other forms of AI, LMMs are likely to encourage automation bias in experts and health-care professionals (and patients, see below). Patients already take significant responsibility for their own care, including taking medicines, improving their nutrition and diet, engaging in physical activity, caring for wounds or delivering injections. AI tools have been projected to increase self-care, including by the use of chatbots, health monitoring and risk prediction tools and systems designed for people with disabilities (1). LMMs could accelerate the trend towards use of AI by patients and laypeople for medical purposes. Individuals have used Internet searches to obtain medical information for two decades. Ethical considerations associated with LMMs and their impact on individuals with disabilities In the past, individuals with disabilities have been excluded from workplaces, educational systems and appropriate medical support (56) and therefore from data sets used to train AI systems. The systems may discriminate against individuals with facial asymmetry, different gesticulation, styles of communication, behaviour and action patterns. The groups that are most severely affected are people with disabilities, cognitive or sensory impairments or autism spectrum disorder (57). Such bias and exclusion may apply to generative AI. For example, LMMs may introduce a negative connotation or sentiment to keywords or phrases associated with “disability” in a patient’s description or biography (58). Chatbots may recognize an individual with a disability as “not alive”, “non-human” or “emotionally flat” because of a different behaviour or pattern of actions. Speech recognition systems may be less accurate for individuals with speech impairments, leading to misinterpretation.

text: 14 Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health. Guidance on large multi-modal models • Inaccurate, incomplete or false statements: As in the use of LMMs by clinicians and health-care professionals, use of LMMs by patients and laypeople is associated with risks of false, biased, incomplete or inaccurate statements, including from AI programmes that claim to provide medical information. The risks are heightened when used by a person without medical expertise, who will have no basis for challenging the response, have no access to another source of information or when used by children (Box 2). Although people have used Internet searches to obtain medical information for several decades, an LMM can provide answers that will appear to be “correct”, with reference only to other LMMs (which carry the same risks) for a quick comparison. • Manipulation: Many LMM-powered chatbot applications have distinct approaches to chatbot dialogue, which is expected to become both more persuasive and more addictive (46), and chatbots may eventually be able to adapt conversational patterns to each user (41).

text: stinct approaches to chatbot dialogue, which is expected to become both more persuasive and more addictive (46), and chatbots may eventually be able to adapt conversational patterns to each user (41). Chatbots can provide responses to questions or engage in conversation to persuade individuals to undertake actions that go against their selfinterest or well-being (12). Several experts have called for urgent action to manage the potential negative consequences of chatbots, noting that they could become “emotionally manipulative” (47,48). One highly publicized case involved a person in Belgium with anxiety, who committed suicide after 6 weeks of intensive conversation with a chatbot (49). • Privacy: Use of LMMs by patients and laypeople may not be private and may not respect the confidentiality of personal and health information that they share. Users of LMMs for other purposes have tended to share sensitive information, such as company proprietary information (50). Data that are shared on an LMM do not necessarily disappear, as companies may use them to improve their AI models (50), even though there may be no legal basis for doing so, even though the data may eventually be removed

A related problem is sharing of information on an LMM with other users of the LMM, whether because the other user specifically requests the LMM to disclose such information (52) or, in the case of one LMM, mistaken disclosure of other people’s chat histories (even if not the substance of their conversations) (53). Thus, if a person’s identifiable medical information is fed into an LMM, it could be disclosed to third parties (54). • Degradation of interactions between clinicians, laypeople and patients: Use of LMMs by patients or their caregivers could change the physician–patient relationship fundamentally. The increase in Internet searches by patients during the past two decades has already changed these relationships, as patients can use the information they find to challenge or seek more information from their health-care provider.

text: 2 Applications and challenges of use of LMMs in health 15 undermine general supportive care, such as human–human interactions when people are often most vulnerable (1). Generally, there is concern that clinical care could be “de-humanized” by AI. • Epistemic injustice: An additional potential consequence of substituting a health-care provider’s judgement with that of an LMM is introduction of epistemic injustice to the patient. “Epistemic injustice” is a “wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a subject of knowledge”, such as a patient in a health-care system (55). One form of epistemic injustice, hermeneutic injustice, occurs when there is a gap in shared understanding and knowledge (so-called “collective interpretive resources”) that puts some people at a disadvantage with respect to their lived experience, social experience or, in the case of health care, their own understanding of their physical or mental condition (55). LMMs, even when trained on large quantities of data, have boundaries with respect to what they can recognize and respond to and the concepts and notions that are outside their vocabulary.

text: dition (55). LMMs, even when trained on large quantities of data, have boundaries with respect to what they can recognize and respond to and the concepts and notions that are outside their vocabulary. If a patient’s experience is not acknowledged or recognized in a clinical setting by an LMM, it can obviate appropriate care from a medical provider, which could harm the patient. This is especially likely for vulnerable groups that are already neglected and underrepresented in data (55), such as people with disabilities (Box 3). • Delivery of health care outside the health-care system: AI applications in health are no longer used exclusively or accessed and used within health-care systems or in home care, as AI technologies for health can be readily acquired and used by nonhealth system entities or simply introduced by a company, such as those that offer LMMs for public use. This raises questions about whether such technologies should be regulated as clinical applications, which require greater regulatory scrutiny, or as “wellness applications”, which require less regulatory scrutiny. At present, such technologies arguably fall into a grey zone between the two categories.
